title: Actions are by intentions
hookLine: actions are only by intentions, and each gets what he intended
tomorrow: a stranger walks in and asks what he already knows. why?

cards: Two people stand at the same Saturday food drive, in the same aprons, stacking the same boxes. One came for the families in line. One came for the hours on a form.
From the parking lot, nobody could tell them apart. Now a pulpit in Medina. Umar ibn al-Khattab stands up and repeats something he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say.
It's about people on the road of the hijrah, the migration to Medina. Same road, same dust, same days of walking. And the Prophet says they didn't all arrive in the same place.

teach.b: Here's the report, in paraphrase, as Sahih al-Bukhari opens with it: actions are only by intentions, and each person gets only what they intended.

So whoever's hijrah was for Allah and His Messenger, their hijrah is for Allah and His Messenger. And whoever's hijrah was for some gain of this world, or a woman to marry, their hijrah is for what they set out for.
Listen to how the sentence is built.

teach.h: ONE GOAL SAID TWICE, ONE NOT AGAIN.
teach.b: For the first traveler, it says the goal twice, word for word. For the second, it doesn't name the goal again at all: just, what he set out for. One road, two journeys, and the difference never showed on anyone's feet.
The word inside the line is niyyah, intention.
One thing to tell a friend tonight: in Islamic law, intention is how one act becomes two. A bath, or the washing a Muslim does before prayer. Skipping breakfast, or a fast.
The intention is what tells them apart. Al-Nawawi's bag of foundations opens here, on the part of every deed only Allah and the doer can see.

how: Muslims make an intention before prayer, a fast or the washing for prayer; scholars hold that it lives in the heart, and schools differ on whether to also say it quietly.

games.q: what does “actions are by intentions” mean?
o: good actions matter more than what you meant by them
a plan only counts once you have carried it out
what you mean by a deed decides what it counts as

games.q: the first hadith — tap the pairs.
p: gets what he set out for

s: an intention only counts if you say it out loud
it lives in the heart. saying it can help you notice it, and schools differ on whether to say it.
in the report, the worldly traveler's goal isn't repeated
the first goal is said twice, word for word. the second is only 'what he set out for'.
on the road, you could tell the two travelers apart
same road, same dust. only the intention separated them.

games.q: you volunteer at a food drive partly because it looks good on an application. a friend says that ruins it. what fits the first hadith?
o: look at what you mean by it, and set the intention before you start.
quit: if any part is for the application, none of it counts.
keep going and don't think about why: the food arrives either way.
games.why: the hadith doesn't send anyone home. it says each person gets what they intended, so the first move is to look, and to set it.

practice: Choose the next ordinary thing you'll do after this: washing a cup, opening a laptop, calling someone back. Say quietly, in a few plain words, what you're doing it for.
The intention lives in the heart; the words just help you notice it. Then sit with that one sentence for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Actions are by intentions: the opening words of al-Nawawi's first hadith. Niyyah, intention, is the word at its center, the reason one act can be two.

orig.note: Arabic: actions are only by intentions. niyyat is the plural of niyyah.

carryVoice: For the road, two seconds before anything: what did I intend? Day three of the last range, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1 (Umar on the pulpit: actions are by intentions; the two hijrahs)
